item.content:encoded:
This is OFF Brand – a newsletter by Koto, a global crew of brand thinkers and makers: designers, strategists, writers, and art directors working across five cities worldwide.

Here, we unpack the messy, brilliant world of branding, diving into everything from naming systems to interfaces, color palettes to campaign thinking, and strategy to storytelling.

Our objective is to be your trusted voice on all things brand. To earn that trust we draw not only on our own experiences, but on those of our peers, clients, experts and beyond. You can expect practical tips, actionable insights, useful frameworks and inspirational examples.

Our last issue hit 10.9K subscribers. If you’re one of them, hats off for having great taste. If not, now’s your chance to jump in and stay in the loop. Hit subscribe, and OFF Brand will land straight in your inbox.

Now, let’s discuss branding…

Thanks for reading OFF Brand. Subscribe to receive new posts.

What you’ll learn about brand differentiation

– What is differentiation?
– Why it matters, now more than ever?
– How differentiation builds on a truth of your business?
– How differentiation helps you stand out from your category?
– How differentiation gives your audience a reason to care?
– When will differentiation ever end? (Spoiler alert: never.)

Why differentiation matters

We live in a world overflowing with options. From the supermarket shelves to SaaS, consumers are constantly being asked to make a choice. And the more comparable products, services, and brands on offer, the harder it is for that choice to be made. An abundance of options begins to feel more like a burden than a blessing. Consumers hesitate, second-guess, leads go cold, and carts are abandoned.

Psychologist Barry Schwartz calls this all-too-familiar experience the paradox of choice. This is the idea that the more options a person has, the more difficult it is to make that decision and the less satisfied people feel with the decision they end up making. This isn't just because the act of choosing requires more cognitive effort when there are more options, but because people are also likely to experience FOMO and ultimately regret the choice they’ve made.

“Learning to choose is hard. Learning to choose well is harder. And learning to choose well in a world of unlimited possibilities is harder still, perhaps too hard.”

— Barry Schwarz, ‘The Paradox of Choice: Why More is Less’

The slow march towards sameness

Although Schwartz coined the term 'Choice Paralysis' over 20 years ago , today it feels harder than ever before to make satisfying choices

Not only do today's consumers have more choices, but the brands they're being asked to choose between are becoming increasingly difficult to differentiate. Rebrands follow the same trends. Websites and apps use uniform code libraries and UX principles. And in an effort to become more digital-friendly, logos are designing out what once made them special.

Everything is gradually converging toward the average, and AI will only accelerate this trend.

In the next edition of this newsletter, we'll dive into how AI is transforming design, including the ways we at Koto are using it to push our creativity, achieve the previously unimaginable, and work more effectively. However, it's important to remember that AI, at its core, is a technology that recognises and learns from patterns. While it can be used to spark or execute new ideas, it also makes it easier to replicate what’s already been done. Used unimaginatively, AI will proliferate brand replicas.

It’s time to think different

The good news: your brand can be the key to helping consumers overcome choice paralysis. From a commercial point of view investments in differentiation deliver returns that far exceed their initial investment, driving market share growth and unlocking premium pricing strategies for your business.

But what actually is differentiation? Miriam Webster defines it as ‘the act or process of differentiating.’ While technically correct, this definition is entirely unhelpful for our current purposes. This is because it suggests that the more different a brand is, the more successful the differentiation. In reality, this is rarely the case.

At Koto we prefer a less prescriptive, yet more practical definition: that a brand’s point of differentiation should answer three relative questions. Does it build on a truth at the heart of a business? Is it distinctive within the category? Will it feel compelling to the audience?

In this edition of OFF Brand we'll guide you through what it takes to answer these three criteria.

What will soon become clear is that differentiation is not a one-size-fits all strategy. There are countless choices open to a brand and business on its journey to differentiation. But hopefully, with the help of this newsletter, you will feel empowered, not paralysed, by this abundance of choice.

Differentiation is true to your business

Differentiation is more than just optics; it’s a strategic, intentional process that should be rooted in the truth of your business. Without this foundation, your brand’s point of difference risks feeling disconnected from the actual experience you deliver, ultimately undermining your brand’s integrity and disappointing your customers.

Yet while it should be rooted in truth, brand differentiation isn’t an exact science. There’s no single objective factor or universal formula to follow. Instead, there are several key starting points to explore when differentiating a brand.

At Koto, we kick off most projects with what we call an 'immersion': a dedicated research process that combines interviewing internal and external stakeholders, reviewing audience insights, and assessing cultural and category trends. This helps us uncover the essential truths that will serve as the foundation for a brand’s differentiation.

Before you dive into an immersion of your own, there are a number of ways into uncovering a truth for your brand.

Starting point 01: Product

A great place to begin, and perhaps the most obvious, is your product. This could include everything from its unique features or attributes, to how the product is designed or made, or even where it’s from – think ‘Swiss design’ or ‘Made in America’. However, whatever sets your product apart, it’s crucial to identify a differentiator that doesn’t just stand out against the category as it exists today, but also one that your competitors can’t easily replicate in the future too.

Some questions to consider:

  • Is your product a market-leader? (Think ‘No one got fired for buying IBM’ )

  • Does your product interface with the other products your consumers own or use? (Think Slack)

  • Is your product more powerful or does it perform to a high standard? (Think Porsche)

  • Is there an ownable technology that powers your product? (Think Dyson)

  • Does your product meet rigorous technical standards or is it reliable? (Think Volvo)

  • Is your product made in a significant geographic location? (Think Swatch)

Starting point 02: Experience

Rather than going spec for spec with competitor products, another way to find your truth is by unpacking the experience you offer your customers. This is relevant to both physical and digital experiences, and could relate to something that’s fundamental to your offering or any extra value-added services that enhance the customer experience.

Some questions to consider:

  • Is there an ownable aspect of your user experience or interface? (Think Tinder’s swipe mechanic)

  • Do you serve a particular need or desire, above all else? (Think Amazon Prime’s commitment to convenience)

  • Is your after-care support better than anyone in your category? (Think Applecare)

  • Do you have an outstanding warranty or customer promise? (Think Rimowa)

  • Can users customize or tailor your product to be their own?(Think Tylko)

  • Do you have a loyalty or rewards scheme that adds value to your offer? (Think Amex)

Starting point 03: Price

Price differentiation is a tricky strategy that can easily turn into a zero-sum game, increasing your market share at the expense of your profit margins. However, when approached strategically and in the right context it can still be effective, especially when price sensitivity is a major factor for customers. To avoid diminishing your brand’s perception, it’s best to reframe price as a reflection of value, not quantifiable cost.

Some questions to consider:

  • Is everything about your business laser-focussed on budget and bottom-line? (Think Hans Brinker)

  • Do you have a pricing strategy that strips back all the added extras? (Think Ryanair)

  • Do you have a commitment to price matching? (Think John Lewis’ ‘Never knowingly undersold’)

  • Is your price iconic or fixed? (Think Poundland or Dollar Tree)

  • Do you offer economies of scale when customers purchase in bulk? (Think Costco)

  • Does your business model or infrastructure challenge a price monopoly? (Think Warby Parker)

Starting point 04: Channel

Where a brand shows up can be a key factor in differentiation, shaping how people perceive it through association. This goes beyond where its products or services are sold – whether through D2C models or in high-end department stores. The non-transactional spaces a brand occupies, for example through advertisements or sponsorships, will also play a significant role in shaping the associations it builds over time.

Some questions to consider:

  • Does your brand turn up in convenient places, where people need it most? (Think McDonald’s)

  • Or is your brand in a location where people visit with specific intention? (Think Ikea)

  • Does your brand turn up in exclusive, or culturally relevant places? (Think LVMH)

  • Is your brand an intermediary or marketplace? (Think eBay)

  • Does your business model side-step conventional distribution? (Think Dollar Shave Club)

  • Does your business currently or does it have capacity to sponsor cultural events? (Think T Mobile)

Starting point 05: Purpose

A purpose defines your company's reason to exist, beyond making money. Top of mind are brands that differentiate through an altruistic cause. But we can also think of purpose more broadly, as the transformational changes a brand seeks to create in people's lives, culture, or the world at large.

Some questions to consider:

  • Is your business known for its social or environmental commitments? (Think Patagonia)

  • Does your product or service cause less harm than your competitors? (Think The Body Shop)

  • Does your brand stand against the malpractices of the category? (Think Tony’s Chocolonely)

  • Does your brand stand in support of a defined group? (Think Dove)

  • Does your business set out to improve or replace a fundamental aspect of society? (Think Coinbase)

  • Will your business change perceptions or habits of your consumer group? (Think Backmarket)

Where to start?

Many of the starting points we touched upon above can be true of your brand at once. For some brands there will be a clear differentiator to double down on, but most will have multiple viable starting points. And as we discussed at the beginning of this newsletter, having many options can make any decision difficult.

In the next chapters, we’ll focus on the context of your category and your audience’s preference in differentiation. These factors may help guide your decision, but they won’t dictate exactly how your brand should differ. As Al Ries and Jack Trout state in The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing, "There is no objective reality. There are no facts. There are no best products. There are only better according to certain metrics."

Perception is reality. Brand differentiation might build on a truth at the heart of your business, but choosing which truth requires conviction. Research can guide you, analysis can inform you, and brand studios like Koto can support you in this decision. But ultimately the final decision is yours to make.

Choice is hard, but choose you must.

Branding is about accepting that you can’t be everything to everyone. Just as excellence comes at a cost, so does successful differentiation. To be known for one thing often means placing less emphasis on other aspects of your business.

“Difference is deviance. Difference is permutation. Difference is a commitment to the unprecedented, which is another way of saying it is a commitment to letting go.”

Different: Escaping the Competitive Herd, Youngme Moon

But choosing a single core point of difference, or a few closely connected truths, can pay off in powerful ways.

Internally, a clear focus allows your teams to make strategic, high-impact investments that drive ROI. Externally, simplifying your message helps capture attention and keeps your brand top of mind, no matter how crowded or competitive the category.

Speaking of which…

Differentiation is distinctive to your category

As humans, we naturally categorize the world around us. It’s a shortcut that helps us make quicker and better decisions based on expectations formed from past experiences. The same principle applies to branding. Think about how store shelves or ecommerce menus organize products into clear, intuitive categories in order to make the shopping experience smoother and more familiar.

Although categorisation might be intuitive, building a brand isn’t about copying every convention of your category. Instead, effective differentiation requires a brand to find the right balance between fitting in and standing out; between leveraging the positive associations of a category while subverting them just enough to create distinction.

But first, which category?

Since distinction is always relative, the first step is to define the category your product or service is expected to belong to. Understanding this context helps reveal the expectations and perceptions people already hold—giving you something to build on, challenge, or creatively subvert.

If you're in a well-established category, this is often straightforward. But even if your offering feels entirely new, there are still existing conventions you can tap into. Ask yourself: Who are your competitors? What product, service, or behavior might you replace? Does your solution use similar technology or deliver similar outcomes? Where might it sit on store shelves, ecommerce sites, comparison blogs, or at trade shows?

Answering these kinds of questions helps you find your starting point, and understand how you can stand apart.

3 strategies for category distinction

In “Different: Escaping the Competitive Herd”, Harvard professor Youngme Moon argues that the more competitive a category is, the more brands tend to resemble each other. Think how a slew of vegan alternatives adopted the attitude of Oatly or how many B2B SaaS products have uncannily similar illustration styles.

Written in a refreshingly readable style befitting of the title ‘different’, in one chapter she describes standing in the cereal aisle. She sees healthy cereals. Natural cereals. Cereal for kids. More fibre. Less sugar. More of this. Less of that. Everything is different in the same ways. Every brand plays by the expected rules of cereal.

The book continues to outline three strategies for category differentiation: Reverse Brands, Breakaway Brands, and Hostile Brands.

While not an exhaustive list, these approaches offer a solid range of ways to stand out. So let’s explore them in more detail.

01. Reverse brands

Reverse brands embrace the philosophy that less is more. They remove unnecessary features to simplify their offering. On the face of it this might sound reductive, but as Moon explains: "reverse brands create a kind of tilt in the surface—of progress, of evolution, of expectation. They draw us down a divergent path by applying pressure in exactly the place where we least anticipate it."

Take IKEA. Customers are asked to locate their own furniture in a warehouse, transport it home, then assemble it themselves. The experience isn’t what you’d consider aspirational. Yet, at the same time, IKEA offers free childcare and an on-site restaurant serving famous Swedish meatballs. This contradiction highlights the core behavior of reverse brands: "It looks to create a symbiosis of elements that we’ve been trained to believe don’t belong together. The idea is to be an oxymoron, and an agreeable one at that."

Reverse brands are also particularly powerful at cutting through in categories rife with feature fatigue, instead reminding customers why they are interested in a product or service in the first place. Apple, for example, have elevated their brand beyond a like-for-like comparison in computing power - GB storage, RAM, CPU and so on. Instead Apple’s brand reminds people that computing power is a means to an end, an experience defined by the brand’s three principles - ‘simple’, ‘human’, ‘creative’.

02. Hostile brands

In a world defined by seamlessness, Hostile brands introduce new friction into their category. They play harder to get than their competitors, they are more divisive and they make us work harder for their custom.

At first, this strategy feels counterintuitive. But look closely and you’ll begin to see hostile brands everywhere. Marmite tells us if you don’t love the taste, you’ll hate it. Ben and Jerry's champions altruistic causes and isn’t concerned with what anyone thinks about it. Streetwear brands like Supreme or Palace create scarcity, forcing customers to queue for hours for the opportunity to buy a t-shirt. Even Apple can be found behaving with hostility, creating friction whenever users want to repair their devices and asking users to change adapters every few product generations.

Moon puts it this way: “Hostile brands erect barriers to consumption, barriers that could in many ways be considered tests of our affiliation.” In weeding out indifference, they ensure the consumers that remain are engaged, curious or devout. And by standing firm and refusing to concede these brands also feel more authentic, achieving cult-like status.

03. Breakaway brands

The previous examples show how brands position themselves within a category. Breakaway brands, however, intentionally place themselves outside of their conventional category.

Breakaway brands respect the power of categorization whilst also understanding it is an arbitrary social construction. They defy expectations to create something novel and intriguing.

Moon gives a few examples of breakaway brands: Nest, which moved from thermostats to computation. Swatch, which redefined watches as fashion accessories. And Sony’s Aibo, which was marketed as a pet not a technology, permitting users to view any technological failures as personality quirks they might otherwise expect from a dog.

An example of a breakaway brand Koto helped build is Need. Need might conventionally be seen as a cancer insurance platform. However, in the Korean market where Need first launched, most customers already have health insurance. To avoid prompting the difficult question - ‘Why buy what I’ve already got?’ - Koto instead positioned Need as the world’s first ‘Cancer protection system’. This shift allowed customers to view Need’s product as a new opportunity to invest in their future health and create emotional security, rather than an insurance against the worst-case scenario.

Warning: a little distinction goes a long way

While some brands may benefit from being truly original, differentiation is rarely about being as different as possible. Disregarding established category norms or expected design tropes can confuse consumers. Take Jaguar’s recent rebrand as a case in point. Not only did it not build on an important truth at the heart of the carmaker’s business: its heritage. The rebrand felt uncanny because it didn’t even seem like it came from a car brand at all.

Jaguar has strong brand recognition, and people know exactly what they do. However, for a start-up or lesser-known brand, moving too far away from a category can cause even greater risk, and leave them out of the consideration set entirely. As a result, these brands spend more time explaining what they do, instead of why they’re different.

For similar reasons, Bloom’s CSO Ed Hayes champions the power of slow disruption in his article ‘We need to talk about disruption’ for Creative Review. “The slower disruptors don’t just add value to consumers”, he writes, “they make sense business-wise, since they’re far more likely to achieve longevity. Brands that aggressively enter a category at breakneck speed don’t usually last.” In the long run, less proves more.

Erring on the side of caution when it comes to category differentiation, however, doesn’t always lead to conservative brands. Take the rise of so-called DGAF brands: such as Duolingo’s ‘Wholesome unhinged’ mascot, or Nutter Butter’s fever-dream of a TikTok feed. Both have achieved significant levels of differentiation without stepping outside the boundaries of their respective categories. Instead they’ve achieved this through creative expressions that resonate with people emotionally, something we will explore in the next chapter of this newsletter.

Differentiation is compelling to your audience

Differentiation isn’t about your business, it’s about your audience. So whatever truth you've decided will set your business apart or however you’ve decided to position yourself within the market, people will only care if it’s relevant and meaningful to them. The best brands appeal to both reason and emotion to do just this.

The power of emotion

Conventional wisdom suggests that decisions are best made rationally: by weighing options, balancing pros and cons, and arriving at a logical conclusion. Emotions, by contrast, are seen as irrational forces that cloud judgment. Keeping emotions in check, so the story goes, leads to better decision-making.

Recent research, however, has fundamentally challenged this view.

Psychologist Daniel Kahneman and his team won a Nobel Prize for a study revealing that most people make financial decisions based on emotions and personal experiences rather than logic. Kahneman's research found that emotions drive about 90% of our decision-making, with logic influencing only around 10%. Further studies support this, showing that emotions help us make quicker, more relevant decisions that align with our needs and desires, and even strengthen our commitment to those choices over time.

In this same way, brands that also connect with consumers on an emotional level can drive preference and even build loyalty beyond the point of purchase.

The brand ladder: a model to uncover the emotional value of your business

Created by Professor Kevin Lane Keller in his book ‘Strategic Brand Management’, the ‘Brand ladder’ has become one of branding’s most widely used tools to help businesses understand and strengthen their emotional positioning. At Koto, we tend to use a version of the brand ladder that slightly deviates from Keller’s original model, but operates on the same principle.

Think of the brand ladder as a way to illustrate the different levels of value your brand provides. At the bottom, you'll find basic attributes and functionalities; similar to the truth(s) of your business that we discussed in the first chapter of this newsletter. As you travel upwards, however, the ladder begins to reveal emotional benefits. It is these benefits that feel more meaningful and compelling to the consumer.

As with all models, this is just one of many tools that can spark ideas. But what the brand ladder is particularly good at is bringing about a shift in perspective - from focussing on what the business offers, to how that offering resonates emotionally with customers.

Case studies: from functional to emotional value

Here are some Koto case studies that explore how we at Koto have supported clients in bringing about this shift in their brand story: away from what they do, and towards how it feels for their customers.

🍭 Fluz

From functional value: A do-it-all Fintech

Loyalty program, banking app, social network: Fluz is easy to use but not so easy to define. To stand out in a saturated Fintech market, the strategic challenge was to uncover the value these individual features create together.

To emotional value: ’Life on Max’

Fluz helps everyone maximize their money, a state of mind we celebrated in the brand idea ‘Life on Max’. This idea led to a design system with candy-colored gradients, bold ‘Greed Condensed’ fonts and art direction that brought to life the magic of maximal.

🐩 Dis-loyalty (Ennismore Hotels)

From functional value: A new loyalty program

Ennismore owns a diverse collection of hotels across various locations. With a new travel and food loyalty program, they aimed to encourage customers to explore more of their portfolio.

To emotional value: ‘Beat boring’

Introducing Disloyalty, a curated travel and food membership that breaks habits by rewarding firsts. This program was built around the brand idea ‘Beat boring’, daring hotel-goers to think differently about where they eat and stay through an expressive design system, energetic motion, and defiant copy.

🤖 Uniqode

From functional value: Enterprise-grade QR codes

QR codes are no longer just those janky little things that you download from the internet. Today the largest companies in the world rely on them for the successful management of their daily operations. In the world of QR-codes, Uniqode offers unrivalled security, support and scalability making it the first, and arguably the only, platform that was built to be enterprise ready.

To emotional value: ‘From IRL to URL’

QR codes enable a smooth transition between the physical and online worlds with just one click. We visualized this idea through the tactile craft of stitching, symbolizing the connection of two worlds with a simple needle and thread. This concept became the core of our visual identity, highlighting Uniqode’s ability to help businesses move effortlessly between IRL and URL and back again.

The enduring power of simple ideas

A compelling story links a brand’s functional value to its emotional appeal. The simpler the story, the more powerful it becomes.

Here the challenge is finding the right balance – distilling an idea so that it’s intuitive and memorable for customers and immediately useful for internal teams, in a way that doesn’t feel reductive or generic. At Koto, we use a litmus test to ensure an idea’s simplicity endures: “Could a 10-year-old understand this idea?” If the answer is ‘yes’, then we are on the right track.

When and how to test what is emotionally compelling to users (if at all)

In this section of OFF Brand, we’ve made the case for crafting emotionally compelling brand experiences. At this point, it might be tempting to simply ask customers what they like, value, or want. But this approach is ill-advised.

While user insights and cultural analysis are valuable tools, directly asking consumers about their preferences often produces answers rooted in the familiar. The opinions you receive will skew toward what's already available in the market, often echoing what your competitors are doing. What’s new or different can feel unfamiliar, even uncomfortable, making it harder for consumers to articulate a desire for it. This is particularly a problem insofar as your strategic point of difference should be future-facing, setting the direction of your business for the next 5-10 years and beyond.

User testing should never replace internal conviction about the direction of your brand. However, once you’ve clearly defined your strategic intent, testing becomes a useful tool. Here you’re not asking your customers about their preference in general. You’re asking: Which execution best delivers on idea X or evokes emotion Y?

In short: the goal isn’t to let users define your brand’s future, but to ensure the creative expression lands with the intended impact.

Differentiation is never done

So you’ve come this far. You’ve identified the key truth that will distinguish your business. You’ve defined your strategic position within your category. You’ve now pinpointed the emotional value that will make your brand compelling. But this is just the beginning.

Once decided upon, you’ll want to commit your point of differentiation to paper across your brand strategy. It will then serve as the guiding intent at the core of your business, informing every decision it makes, both internally and externally.

If you’ve read the second edition of OFF Brand, What is Brand Strategy and Why Your Company Needs One, you’re probably already familiar with this concept. If not, open it in a new tab and give it a read once you’re done here.

What we want to emphasize in this newsletter is that, through consistent repetition over time, your brand will steadily reinforce its point of difference, ultimately securing a distinct place in the minds and hearts of your audience.

What’s different today becomes normal tomorrow.

Beating the same drum to reinforce your point of difference is crucial. But eventually that rhythm must evolve. As your business grows, so must your brand. Your offering may expand, or your core strengths may shift. And with that evolution, the positioning that once fit perfectly may no longer reflect the scale or direction of your business.

Your most significant change, however, is likely happening outside the four walls of your business.

We, as humans, have an innate tendency to take for granted what once delighted us. This idea is known as the hedonic treadmill. Historical examples include major technological breakthroughs that are now seen as everyday utilities: running water, electricity, the internet, smartphones. But the hedonic treadmill is all around us, and over time it will affect how compelling your point of differentiation will feel to customers.

To put it simply: a company might build a brand around a specific point of differentiation. Customers respond positively, but over time, competitors imitate this point of differentiation until it becomes standard across the category. Customer satisfaction recalibrates. The standards for standing out in the category rise and what once felt remarkable is now ordinary. That company must now refine or redefine its point of differentiation.

Returning to the beginning is not starting again

Rediscovering how your business can stand out will mean going back over the ideas explored in the earlier chapters of this newsletter. This time, you'll be looking at them with more clarity and a new perspective.

So whilst your point of differentiation may need to evolve, it’s important to recognise the role it’s played in getting your brand to where it is today. As it’s what people currently associate with your brand, any shift should feel like a natural progression, not a break, from that foundation.

It’s important to note that growing up doesn’t necessitate getting boring. There’s a common misconception that as brands scale for mass appeal, they must shed the uniqueness that fueled their early success and become more vanilla. We’ve seen this with rebrands from the likes of Robinhood to BackMarket, the latter a step away from Koto’s original work 5 years ago. In both cases, once-disruptive brands toned down their distinctiveness with the ambition of going mainstream. At Koto we believe it isn’t just unnecessary, it’s counterproductive. The result is a strategic loss of identity, making them blend in with the very incumbents they once stood apart from.

In the fourth edition of OFF Brand - “Brand Evolution or Revolution? Knowing Why and When” - we explored what’s involved in refreshing an established brand. The key takeaways still apply here: standing out isn’t something you solve once. It’s a continual process of refinement. As your brand grows, progress doesn’t mean letting go of what works. It means pushing it further, continuing to build on your new strengths and existing equity in tandem. Because your point of difference isn’t a temporary tactic you should grow out of, it’s a core asset that should grow with you.

Wrapping up

In this edition of OFF Brand, we’ve dived into the topic of differentiation. An ongoing, complex and deeply personal journey for any brand that can roughly be boiled down to three questions:

  • Does it build on a truth at the heart of a business?

  • Is it distinctive within the category?

  • Will it feel compelling to the audience?

Deep-dive further with more reads

To further enhance your brand’s ability to answer these three questions, you might also want to dig in to the following resources:

  • Something shorter to skim: “Are rebrands starting to look the same? The challenges defining commercial design” - by Elizabeth Goodspeed, for It’s Nice That

  • Something longer to read: “Different: Escaping the Competitive Herd” - by YoungMe Moon

  • Something to watch: ‘Mark Ritson on defending differentiation - IGNITE 2023’ for Kantar

Let us know what you think

Hit reply or comment:

  • What challenges or opportunities have you come across when differentiating your brand?

  • What resonated with you the most?

  • What else could we have talked about when it comes to brand differentiation?

  • Any suggestions for our next newsletter?

See you in a few weeks for the next edition of OFF Brand. Let’s hope it’s different.

item.title: The invisible hand of brand in the gaming world
item.description: You’ve opened an email about branding in gaming—an often underestimated force behind the biggest cultural hits. Let’s explore why some titles become icons while others disappear.

item.content:encoded:
This is OFF Brand, a newsletter by Koto. We’re designers, strategists, and writers working across five global studios to build brands that stand the test of time.

Branding in gaming goes far beyond logos and marketing—it's the backbone of a game's universe. It shapes how players experience, engage with, and stay hooked on a title. From world-building and game mechanics to monetization strategies and community-building, branding drives every touchpoint and keeps a game culturally relevant long after launch.

In this edition, we’re diving deep into how branding shapes the gaming experience—and what makes certain titles iconic. You’ll see plenty of game references, genres, and mechanics that might be new to you, but trust us—it’s worth the ride. Whether you’re a developer, marketer, or just curious, you’ll walk away with a fresh perspective on branding. Not into video games? Stick around—these lessons on loyalty and cultural impact go far beyond the screen.

We’ve already brought together 10K brand enthusiasts like you, and 1.1K new readers have signed up since our last issue—so, thanks for reading! If someone shared this with you, why not join us? Subscribe now and get future editions straight to your inbox.

Alright. Let’s talk about gaming brands.

Thanks for reading OFF Brand. Subscribe to receive new posts.

What you’ll learn about branding in gaming

– How brand strategy drives game longevity
– Why world-building starts with brand strategy
– Naming’s role in franchise success
– How brand shapes communities and culture

Why branding matters in gaming

In gaming, brand isn’t a layer—it is the experience. More than a logo or a trailer, it shapes worlds, drives gameplay, and builds culture.

On mobile—where players jump into quick, daily sessions—brand sparks instant connection and fuels lasting loyalty. It’s how players discover, engage, and spend, turning apps into habits and titles into trends.

Brand makes players care. And care is currency.

From iconic names to franchise empires, brand turns a single release into a cultural force. Console, PC, or mobile—a strong brand doesn’t just build audiences. It builds legacies.

Let’s break it down.

Brand strategy: the blueprint for world-building and longevity

Before a single frame is rendered, a character designed, or a gameplay loop finalized, brand strategy is already shaping the game’s DNA. Unlike tech products, where branding clarifies function, gaming brands are built around immersion—defining the emotional and narrative experience before the player even presses start.

Players come to games for a promised fantasy. The name—more on this later—along with the first glimpse of a game sets expectations in their imagination. From there, the game must fulfill or exceed that vision.

Tech brands signal a category—fintech, AI, SaaS. Gaming brands signal an entire world. Whether it’s fantasy, shooter, or strategy, players should feel the genre before they even understand the mechanics. The best gaming brands don’t just tell you what a game is; they make you feel it.

Brand strategy isn’t just about emotion or genre—it’s about structure. It aligns game mechanics, art direction, storytelling, and character design to shape a lasting experience. In mobile gaming, this structure extends into every tap and swipe—from the app store icon to the onboarding screen. Brand signals compress into micro-moments: visuals that pop in crowded marketplaces and gameplay loops that hook players instantly—like Clash Royale’s rapid duels or Candy Crush’s cascading combos.

More than a theme, it’s the blueprint that holds a game’s universe together.

Key areas of influence include:

  • World-building — Define rules, mythology, and tone. Mobile games excel at fast, vivid lore, while PC and console titles offer vast, evolving universes.

  • Character & environment design — How heroes, factions, and settings reinforce brand identity

  • Gameplay mechanics as brand identity — Iconic mechanics build lasting recall. Mobile games shine with compact loops—like Subway Surfers’ endless run—just as console classics are known for signature moves like Mario Kart’s banana peels or Metal Gear Solid’s cardboard box—become brand signatures. In the indie space, Palworld carved out its own identity by fusing creature collection with survival shooter mechanics, while Helldivers 2 made friendly-fire chaos a brand signature—its satirical war propaganda aesthetic fueling community-driven storytelling and meme culture

  • Franchise sustainability — Building worlds that support sequels, spin-offs, and cultural extensions

With gameplay innovation plateauing, some studios have leaned on repackaging familiar mechanics into new addictive loops to boost retention and revenue. It’s a quick fix—but one that comes at a cost. When these systems aren’t grounded in the game’s world or brand identity, they create friction. And friction breaks immersion.

Brand strategy prevents that. It aligns creative direction with commercial design—ensuring monetization flows from the logic of the universe, not around it. When done well, systems like gacha pulls, battle passes, or time-limited drops feel embedded. Not imposed.

Mobile titles often lead here. The strongest examples integrate monetization into progression and play—seamlessly extending the fantasy without disrupting it. But when console and PC titles apply aggressive tactics that undercut their own narrative or aesthetic, players notice. And they push back. Immersion is the promise. Anything that breaks it feels like betrayal.

This is the power of brand strategy. It brings coherence to every touchpoint—visual, mechanical, commercial—and transforms world-building from storytelling into long-term value.

Now, from principle to practice. At Koto, our gaming heads have picked standout titles where brand strategy and universe creation pack real impact and originality.

Take Elden Ring, for example—a brand built on mystique and challenge. FromSoftware’s identity is unmistakable: punishing difficulty, fragmented storytelling, gothic world design. But what set Elden Ring apart wasn’t just its mechanics—it was the decision to bring in George R.R. Martin to shape its lore. Instead of solely relying on their own interpretation of medieval fantasy, FromSoftware tapped into a voice that resonated more naturally with Western audiences. The result? A world that felt richer, more grounded, and instantly compelling.

Though Elden Ring is a new IP, it carries the studio’s DNA. Its lore, non-playable-character (NPC) interactions, and map design all reinforce FromSoftware’s brand—ensuring players know exactly what they’re getting (and suffering through).

A single block can build a world. That’s the magic—and the brand—of Minecraft. Its blocky, lo-fi visuals aren’t a style choice; they are the identity. Simplicity fuels creativity, accessibility, and limitless possibility. But here’s the twist: unlike most games, Minecraft’s brand belongs to the players. Their creations, their stories, their servers—that’s what shapes the game’s identity.

Supercell mastered the formula of strategy-driven chaos with a cartoony edge. Clash of Clans’ brand thrives on community—clan wars, alliances, and real-time strategy forged a social identity. The game’s playful, exaggerated character design and quick-hit gameplay are instantly recognizable, creating a brand that’s both competitive and accessible. Its advertising, often humorous and character-driven, extends the world beyond the screen.

ustwo games Monument Valley is a masterclass in brand through art and feeling. The game's brand identity is calm, mysterious, and meditative, with its impossible architecture and Escher-inspired puzzles. Soft colors, atmospheric music, and a subtle narrative create a deeply emotional experience. The simplicity is intentional—the brand is about beauty in minimalism.

You don’t just play The Last of Us—you feel it. Fear in every abandoned street. Loss in every quiet moment. Its brand is built on emotional storytelling, where survival mechanics and atmospheric world-building blur the line between game and experience. Crumbling cities, nature reclaiming man’s ruins, and raw human connection define its identity—across games, and now, a TV series that hits just as hard.

If you’ve driven through San Andreas, you know—GTA is the ultimate brand of chaos. Its satirical, hyper-stylized version of America is one of gaming’s most distinct and consistent brand identities.

Rockstar owns its space with:

  • Freeform chaos as a gameplay signature.

  • Iconic radio stations, reinforcing immersion.

  • Cinematic storytelling with dark humor, separating it from other open-world crime games.

  • GTA Online, transforming the brand into a persistent virtual world.

Strong brand strategy goes beyond aesthetics—it shapes every layer of a game whatever the platform, from world-building and mechanics to character design and storytelling. The key is crafting a cohesive, emotionally rich universe that seamlessly ties together gameplay, narrative, promotion, and merchandising.

Successful worlds establish one or multiple strong identity markers, such as:

  • Deep lore & storytelling – The Witcher, The Last of Us

  • Signature gameplay mechanics – Mario’s jump, Metal Gear’s stealth, Soulslike combat, Angry Birds slingshot physics

  • Entire virtual worlds & sandbox freedom – Minecraft, Grand Theft Auto, Fortnite, and Roblox—which have essentially redefined the “Third Place” for youth gaming, a space once dominated by Massively Multiplayer Online (MMO) games

  • Genres so distinct they become their own – Dark Souls and the rise of Soulslike games, Clash Royale defined the mobile real-time strategy genre

The best gaming brands don’t just make games—they build worlds players recognize, feel, and lose themselves in for days.

Naming a game: the first—and most crucial—brand moment

A well-crafted brand strategy is the foundation of world-building, ensuring coherence, emotional depth, and a clear path to franchise growth. But what’s a great game without a name that resonates?

Before players experience a game, they experience its name. The right name isn’t just a label—it’s the first spark of curiosity, the start of an emotional connection, and the foundation for something bigger. It has the power to intrigue, inspire, and define a franchise’s future. In other words: it’s an invitation.

At Koto, we’re passionate about finding great company names (read more about our secret sauce here), and all our hard-earned learnings apply just as well to the gaming industry. So we thought—why not share a few key recommendations on how to approach game naming strategically?

You should consider three core dimensions:

  1. Does it reflect the world you’re building?

A name should instantly transport players—hinting at the universe they’re about to enter and the emotions they’ll experience within it.

Genshin Impact crackles with cosmic power and destiny. Genshin, steeped in Eastern mythology, evokes divine origins. Impact hits with action and high stakes. Together, it’s a celestial collision—epic, urgent, unforgettable.

Dark Souls signals punishment, struggle, and depth—perfect for a challenging, atmospheric RPG with cryptic lore. The contrast of “Dark” and “Souls” conveys both despair and the spiritual theme of death and rebirth, reinforcing the game’s mechanics and narrative.

Valorant suggests precision, boldness, and skill—perfect for a competitive tactical shooter. “Valor” evokes heroism, reinforcing the high-stakes, skill-based nature of esports. But its biggest win? It’s a made-up word that’s easy to say in any language, giving Riot Games total searchability and a name no one else can own.

Red Dead Redemption blends the Western outlaw fantasy with deeper themes of morality, revenge, and change. “Red Dead” establishes the frontier setting, while “Redemption” suggests transformation. The alliteration makes it memorable, and its structure supports franchise expansion (Red Dead Revolver, Red Dead Redemption 2).

  1. Is it unique, ownable, and memorable?

Great names cut through the noise—distinct, unforgettable, and undeniably yours.

Hollow Knight is poetic yet simple, reinforcing its indie, cult-classic appeal. The juxtaposition of “Hollow” (emptiness, loneliness) and “Knight” (heroism, duty) captures the game’s melancholic, heroic tone.

God of War is primal, direct, and instantly evocative—signaling epic scale, divine conflict, and mythology. The title doesn’t just describe the protagonist—it establishes a world ruled by violent gods and warriors.

Brawl Stars is bold and brash, packed with energy and attitude. “Brawl” evokes raw, chaotic combat, while “Stars” adds flair and fame—heroes clashing for glory. The sharp, two-word punch mirrors the game’s fast-paced, hero-driven battles and colorful multiplayer mayhem.

Celeste is a single-word name that captures both the game’s literal setting (a mountain) and its emotional journey (climbing as a metaphor for overcoming personal struggles). It has an elegant, lyrical quality, making it memorable and distinct in the indie space.

  1. Does it spark curiosity?

The best names captivate players—teasing what’s inside and making them crave more.

Bioshock suggests a fusion of science fiction and horror, core to the game’s identity. The name immediately hints at its retro-futuristic, bioengineering themes—but it also carries a deeper layer. It’s a nod to System Shock, the cult classic that put director Ken Levine on the map, making it an insider reference that resonated with longtime fans while setting the stage for something new.

Half-Life references the scientific concept of radioactive decay, subtly teasing the game’s physics-based mechanics and dystopian setting. It evokes both science and existential dread, fitting the game’s atmosphere and narrative.

Limbo is eerie and enigmatic—a single word loaded with unease. It conjures images of purgatory, the unknown, and the in-between, perfectly setting the tone for its shadowy, unsettling world.

Hades is simple yet powerful—instantly linking to Greek mythology and the underworld. It evokes death, fire, and eternal struggle, all central to its roguelike gameplay and narrative themes.

In the end, a great game name is a promise—a signal of the experience to come.

It should:

  • Reflect the game’s universe and themes—Red Dead Redemption, Dark Souls, The Last of Us

  • Be unique, ownable, and unforgettable—Portal, Celeste, Hollow Knight, Brawl Stars

  • Spark curiosity and anticipation—Bioshock, Half-Life, Bloodborne, Limbo

The best game names don’t just label—they create worlds. They set expectations, spark emotion, and in the rarest cases, become bigger than the game itself. “I’m in Minecraft” isn’t just something players say—it’s proof a name can turn a game into a place people live in.

Wordmark and logo design: the first emotional brand asset

Once the game name is locked, wordmark and logo design become the first visual cue of a game’s identity. It’s a critical moment where the best logos successfully reflect world-building, tone, and differentiation.

Grand Theft Auto's logo is a masterclass in brand storytelling. Its bold, blocky, all-caps design screams urban chaos, rebellion, and street culture—perfectly aligned with GTA’s crime-driven, open-world identity. Decades of consistent visual cues mean that whether it’s GTA III, Vice City, or San Andreas, players instantly recognize the brand’s DNA.

If you’re a true game lover, you must be fond of Link and The Legend of Zelda. Its logo stands as a benchmark for fantasy brand building. Its ornate, fantasy-inspired typography evokes adventure, mythology, and epic storytelling. The iconic sword motif—seen in logos from A Link to the Past to Twilight Princess—reinforces the series' heroic themes and unmistakable identity.

The Angry Birds logo is pure energy—explosive, mischievous, and packed with attitude. The bold, slanted font feels like it’s mid-flight, charging toward chaos. And that iconic red bird face? Pure rage and determination. It captures the game’s slingshot-fueled, feather-flying chaos in a single glance. You don’t just see it—you feel the tension.

The DOOM logo—a true legend in the FPS genre—with its heavy, metallic, 3D-style wordmark, is raw power—loud, aggressive, unstoppable. Forged in fire and chaos, it perfectly captures the game’s mix of sci-fi horror, relentless action, and pulse-pounding metal. You don’t just see it—you feel it: fast, brutal, iconic.

The Street Fighter logo, with its graffiti-like brushstrokes, hits with the same speed and flair as a perfect combo. Bold reds and yellows burst with arcade-era nostalgia, throwing you straight into the heat of battle—Ryu’s Hadouken, Ken’s Shoryuken, Blanka’s electric charge. It’s more than a logo. It’s the sound of quarters dropping and victory screens flashing.

The takeaway for game creators? A strong wordmark isn’t just identification; it’s invitation. The best logos don’t just label a game—they let players feel it. They signal what kind of universe awaits, from GTA’s street-level grit to Zelda’s mythic quests.

Building long-term gaming franchises: the art of sustainable growth

In the gaming world, naming isn’t just a title—it’s a blueprint for expansion. The strongest franchises use naming systems that balance consistency with adaptability, enabling spin-offs, sub-brands, and sequels to feel both fresh and familiar.

Here’s how the best in the industry do it:

Few franchises have mastered this balance as well as Call of Duty. Over the past two decades, Activision has built the game into a cultural juggernaut, developing distinct sub-brands that cater to different playstyles and themes while maintaining a unified brand identity:

  • Call of Duty: Modern Warfare — A tactical, military-focused identity built on realism and contemporary warfare.

  • Call of Duty: Black Ops — A darker, espionage-driven sub-brand steeped in covert operations and psychological warfare.

  • Call of Duty: Warzone — A battle royale extension, adapting to modern multiplayer trends while staying true to the franchise’s DNA.

But keeping a brand this expansive cohesive across premium titles, live services, esports, and marketing is no small feat. That’s where Koto came in.

In a multi-year collaboration with Activision, we redefined the Call of Duty brand architecture, creating a masterbrand system that unifies every title under a clear, structured identity. We developed a new franchise logo, a custom typeface called ‘Hitmarker’, and an adaptable design framework that works across game UI, live events, and marketing—ensuring consistency no matter where fans engage with the brand.

This structure doesn’t just help Call of Duty stay visually cohesive—it future-proofs the brand for new titles, game modes, and spin-offs for years to come. The result? A brand that grows without losing what makes it iconic.

Through its efforts, Ubisoft has kept Assassin’s Creed fresh by tying game titles to historical settings, signaling both narrative shifts and gameplay evolution:

  • Assassin’s Creed II, III, IV — The numbered entries build continuity in the Ezio and Desmond sagas

  • Assassin’s Creed Origins, Odyssey, Valhalla — These entries shift the brand toward historical eras while maintaining the core stealth and adventure identity

  • Assassin’s Creed Mirage — A return to the classic, stealth-focused gameplay of the original AC titles

This approach preserves brand consistency while ensuring each title feels unique.

Japanese icon Nintendo has mastered brand extensions through a flexible, modular naming system that keeps its crown jewel, Mario, at the center while enabling endless genre exploration:

  • Mainline platformers, like Super Mario Bros., Super Mario 64, Super Mario Odyssey. Each signals a new era of platforming innovation

  • Racing spin-offs, like Mario Kart 8 Deluxe keep the core Mario identity while emphasizing arcade-style racing

  • Sports games, like Mario Tennis, Mario Golf, Mario Strikers. They extend Mario’s playful and competitive brand into sports sub-genres

  • RPG sub-series, like Paper Mario, Mario & Luigi: Superstar Saga. They create entirely new gameplay styles while maintaining Mario’s universe

This flexible system allows infinite exploration without losing sight of Mario’s core identity.

Final Fantasy is one of the few franchises that successfully uses a pure numbering system:

  • Final Fantasy I-XVI — Despite radically different settings, characters, and combat systems, the numbered structure gives the series prestige and consistency

  • Final Fantasy VII Remake, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth — Square Enix extends a legendary entry into a multi-game sub-franchise, reinforcing FFVII as a distinct pillar within the larger Final Fantasy universe

The numbering reinforces heritage, while spin-offs build depth without confusing players.

So, after all these examples, what really stands out?

The strongest naming systems do more than sound good—they work. They ensure:

  • Expansion stays clear: Call of Duty: Warzone and Mario Kart grow the brand without confusion.

  • Innovation feels familiar: Final Fantasy blends numbered titles and spin-offs to keep fans engaged.

  • New entries signal direction: Assassin’s Creed Valhalla makes it clear—same world, new adventure.

  • Big brands stay unified: Mario’s name ties wildly different games to one beloved character.

That’s why more studios are shifting from straight numbering to “Name: Subtitle” formats—to prevent players from skipping a game because they think they need to play earlier titles first.

In a crowded market, a smart naming strategy isn’t just branding—it’s about making sure players know exactly where to jump in.

Brand in every player touchpoint

Now close your eyes and think of brand consistency as a cheat code for gaming brands.

A great game isn’t just played—it’s felt, shared, and becomes part of culture. And culture doesn’t grow from randomness. It sticks because of patterns, recognition, and repetition.

That’s what brand consistency does.

In gaming, where players connect through social media, live streams, fan art, and modding, a scattered brand is easy to forget. A strong brand should hit hard in every interaction players have with it.

From teaser trailers to Twitch chats, from subreddit debates to meme-worthy moments—every piece should feel like it belongs in the same world. If not, your brand risks being just another NPC in a crowded game.

Pre-launch hype—building anticipation with intent

The most successful gaming brands understand that building anticipation is an art form. Pre-launch campaigns, beta tests, and expansions must feel like an organic continuation of the brand, setting expectations while deepening emotional investment. The best brands don’t just market—they build worlds players want to return to, even before the game drops.

When Rockstar announced Grand Theft Auto VI, they didn’t need a long-winded campaign or an E3 stage show. They dropped a single teaser image. A cryptic tweet. That was it. And the internet lost its mind. Why? Because GTA as a brand has cultivated decades of trust, cultural weight, and anticipation. Every previous installment reinforced an identity of excess, satire, and sprawling open-world mastery. Players didn’t just want another game—they wanted the next chapter in an ongoing cultural event. Rockstar understands that a brand built on scarcity and impact doesn’t need to shout—it just needs to whisper at the right time.

Epic Games has rewritten the playbook on keeping a game fresh. Fortnite doesn’t follow the traditional “release, sequel, repeat” model. Instead, it reinvents itself every season, injecting new characters, collaborations, and map overhauls that keep players engaged without ever feeling like a hard reset. Whether it’s a Marvel takeover, an Attack on Titan crossover, or a LEGO-themed creative sandbox, Fortnite keeps expanding without diluting its core DNA. It’s not just a battle royale—it’s an evolving entertainment platform where every new season seamlessly extends the brand experience.

Supercell’s Clash Royale nailed pre-launch anticipation by building on Clash of Clans' legacy. Soft launches, YouTuber collabs, and live tournaments drove massive hype. The result? A seamless extension of the Clash universe that hooked millions from day one.

Blizzard’s transition from Overwatch to Overwatch 2 was a lesson in how brand consistency can backfire when not carefully managed. Overwatch earned its loyal fanbase with character-driven storytelling, a vibrant hero roster, and polished teamplay. But Overwatch 2 launched with an identity crisis—was it a sequel, a relaunch, or just a free-to-play update? Mixed messaging shattered clarity and splintered the player base, proving that even beloved brands can lose their way.

In contrast, Diablo IV was a masterclass in staying true to brand DNA. Blizzard embraced Diablo’s iconic pillars—dark, gothic storytelling and deep, brutal gameplay. No confusion, no compromise—just a clear evolution of what fans loved. The result? A smoother, stronger reception. Two games, two strategies—one truth: brand evolution only works when it stays crystal clear.

If Rockstar and Epic master controlled hype cycles, Valve thrives on something rarer: myth-making through silence. No game proves it better than Half-Life 3—the most infamous “never announced” title in gaming history. Valve never confirmed it, yet the Half-Life brand stays alive through whispers, fan theories, and community mods.

It’s a masterclass in branding: by saying nothing, Valve let the players shape the legend. It’s risky—this wouldn’t work for every franchise—but it proves a truth every brand should know: Sometimes, what a game represents can outlive the game itself.

Our key takeaway: hype isn’t just marketing—it’s a brand asset. The strongest gaming brands build anticipation as part of their mythology, turning every touchpoint into an event.

The always-on brand: advertising, social media & fan engagement

Once a game is live, branding shifts from launch buzz to long-term engagement—building emotional connections, fostering player loyalty, and keeping the conversation alive. The strongest gaming brands don’t see post-launch engagement as an afterthought; they create dynamic ecosystems that feed interest, shape discussions, and turn players into brand advocates.

Advertising and social media aren’t just sales channels. Building fandom isn’t about flooding people with promos—it’s about creating a real emotional connection. Players expect brands to be active participants in gaming culture, seamlessly distilling marketing into storytelling, community engagement, and shared experiences.

CD Projekt Red turned Cyberpunk 2077 from disaster to redemption. Through transparency, core fixes, and a sharp marketing push—social media, influencers, paid ads—they flipped the narrative. Phantom Liberty wasn’t just an expansion; it was a statement. Their comeback proves a game’s brand isn’t just about launch—it’s about evolution, persistence, and winning back trust.

Riot Games turns content drops into events. It’s a playbook they’ve perfected over a decade in League of Legends. Every Valorant agent reveal comes with cinematic trailers, animated shorts, and cryptic social teasers—building hype long before the patch lands. Riot doesn’t just release content; it keeps players engaged, making every reveal feel like the next chapter in a story they want to keep playing.

Activision keeps Call of Duty fresh by treating every season like a blockbuster event. By integrating pop culture icons like Godzilla vs. Kong, The Boys, and Nicki Minaj, the franchise stays relevant far beyond gaming circles. Their multi-platform marketing spans Twitch, YouTube, TikTok, and in-game promotions, ensuring every seasonal update attracts new players while keeping veterans engaged.

And on mobile, Candy Crush Saga from King made consistency social. Leaderboards, seasonal events, and social sharing features turned players into promoters, proving that engagement is about experience, not just ads.

Community engagement: fostering digital ecosystems

The strongest brands don’t control conversations—they empower communities to shape them. Digital spaces like Reddit, Discord, and fan-run social media accounts transform passive audiences into active contributors, keeping the brand experience alive between major releases.

Take Elden Ring’s Hidden Lore Community (r/Eldenring). FromSoftware’s minimalist storytelling leaves gaps for players to fill. The result? A fan-driven, ever-evolving narrative where communities work together to decipher lore, craft theories, and uncover secrets long after release. Elden Ring thrives on mystery, and its community-driven engagement turns the game into an ongoing intellectual and social experience.

Minecraft is simple: build, break, create. But what Mojang really built is a platform. By empowering, not restricting, player creativity, Minecraft became more than a game—it became a playground for expression. Mods, custom servers, YouTube empires, TikTok trends—every block placed, every world built expands the brand far beyond Mojang’s own design.

This is Minecraft’s genius: its brand belongs to the players. No roadmap, no rules—just limitless creativity driving a thriving creator economy. Proof that sometimes, the most powerful branding isn’t crafted—it’s set free.

The same goes for mobile games. Just look at Genshin Impact—where fan art battles and deep-dive theory threads light up Discord. miHoYo keeps the hype alive with live streams and creator collabs, turning players into co-authors of the game’s unfolding story.

The learning from all of this? Always-on branding is a dialogue, not monologue.

The best gaming brands don’t stop at launch; they evolve alongside their players, staying rooted in culture and conversation. They don’t just exist—they adapt, expand, and become part of players’ stories.

Brand beyond the game: esports, media, and merchandising

A strong gaming brand isn't just about selling copies—it's about building a lasting universe that extends into culture and daily life. The strongest brands drive continuous engagement by expanding into esports, media, fashion, and real-world experiences. Success isn’t just about gameplay—it’s about building brands players want to live in.

Esports: the competitive engine of a strong brand

Riot Games has proven that esports isn’t just a competitive scene—it’s a global brand amplifier. League of Legends has built one of the most successful esports ecosystems, spanning North America to China, turning tournaments into massive cultural events. The LoL World Championship draws millions of viewers annually, rivaling traditional sports broadcasts in both scale and spectacle.

But staying ahead in the ever-evolving esports landscape requires more than just competition—it demands a brand that evolves with its audience. That’s why Riot partnered with Koto to reimagine the League of Legends APAC-EM League, a newly unified regional competition designed to reignite fan passion and reshape perceptions of APAC as a global force.

Counter-Strike, meanwhile, shows that simplicity and consistency build legends. For over two decades, it has dominated esports by sharpening its core mechanics and staying true to its roots. Its enduring success sends a clear message: sometimes in esports, evolution isn’t about chasing trends—it’s about perfecting what matters.

Franchise expansion: from games to mass media

Gaming brands that embed themselves in culture extend far beyond gameplay. Media adaptations, from films to live experiences, aren't just revenue streams—they are brand amplifiers, expanding reach and deepening loyalty.

  1. Movies & TV adaptations

  • Resident Evil — From a film series to Netflix adaptations, the franchise extends horror beyond gaming into pop culture

  • Halo — With a live-action series, Halo translates its rich sci-fi universe into mainstream entertainment

  • Hitman — With multiple film adaptations, Hitman brings its stealth-action thrills from consoles to the big screen

  1. Theme parks & real-world experiences

  • Angry Birds — Theme parks in Finland and China have transformed this mobile gaming hit into a physical, real-world experience, making the brand more tangible

  • Super Nintendo World — A fully immersive environment where visitors interact with the Mario universe, reinforcing its status as a cultural icon across generations

  • Minecraft: Adventures Made Real – The block-building phenomenon is expanding into physical attractions through a $110M partnership with Merlin Entertainments. With theme parks, hotels, and retail spaces launching in the UK and US by 2027, Minecraft is taking its massive audience beyond the screen

These expansions are more than spin-offs—they are powerful brand-building tools that create lasting cultural connections.

  1. Merchandising & brand collaborations

Merchandising and brand partnerships allow gaming brands to reach new audiences and integrate into everyday life. When done authentically, these collaborations don’t weaken the brand—they make it stronger by expanding its influence in a way that feels natural.

Fortnite has turned in-game branding into cultural currency. From Marvel and DC to LEGO, its partnerships go beyond promotion—they’re pop culture events. Fortnite isn’t just a game; it’s an entertainment hub where brands and players collide in one shared universe.

Pokémon proves that a gaming brand's strongest asset isn't just its software—it's cultural relevance. Merchandise, from trading cards to apparel, drives most of its revenue, embedding the brand into everyday life and making it one of the most enduring franchises ever.

Minecraft extends its brand through collaborations like its fashion line with Lacoste, blending gaming with premium markets while preserving its identity.

As we’ve seen, the most successful gaming brands don’t just create games—they build worlds that reach beyond gameplay into esports, movies, TV, fashion, theme parks, and more. For developers and marketers, the key question isn’t just, “How do we make a great game?” but rather, “How do we create a brand that players want to stay connected to, even when they’re not playing?”

Great gaming brands are more than just products—they become cultural landmarks. They grow with their communities, shape the entertainment industry, and keep players engaged by expanding into new spaces. By thinking beyond the game itself, these brands are setting the standard for the future of interactive entertainment.

Final thoughts: is your brand strong enough to survive?

The gaming industry is more crowded than ever. According to The State of Video Gaming in 2025, Steam released almost as many games per month in 2024 as it did in all of 2014—a clear explosion in content.

Yet, 80% of these releases didn’t even crack $5K in sales, showing just how brutal the fight for attention has become.

AI is changing the landscape, accelerating development and shrinking production cycles from years to months. But while it’s reshaping workflows, it’s also a divisive topic across the industry. Some see it as a game-changer; others see it as a threat. One thing is certain: content development spending has surged 90% since 2017, far outpacing consumer spend growth and flooding the market with new titles.

More games, more noise. With 50+ new titles dropping on Steam every day, standing out isn’t just about innovation—it’s about identity. The games that win aren’t always the most groundbreaking, but the ones with a brand that cuts through. A sharp name, bold key art, and a logo that pops in a crowded storefront can be the difference between a breakout hit and a game that disappears on page three.

Despite the flood of releases, players stick with franchises they trust. In 2024, just five franchises, with lifespans of 6 to 22 years, grabbed 30% of total PC playtime and 43% on PlayStation and Xbox.

The takeaway? A great game isn’t enough. Players need to know instantly why your game matters, what sets it apart, and why it’s worth their time. In a world drowning in content, recognition drives choice.

Similarly, mobile gaming faces the same discovery crisis, with app stores dominated by incumbents and user acquisition costs soaring. Mobile titles struggle for visibility, as the top three games per genre capture over 40% of spending, while titles older than two years account for 70% of total revenue. Even standout successes like Monopoly Go! spent $500M on user acquisition to reach $2B in revenue.

The erosion of discovery has turned platform policies and app store commissions into battlegrounds, with Apple and Google pocketing more profit from mobile games than most publishers combined.

From fan engagement to esports, from merch to platform shifts—we’ve explored it all. But it always comes back to one thing: is your brand strong enough to survive? In an industry where AI accelerates development and players face endless options, only brands with real identity, deep community roots, and cultural impact will stand the test of time.
